Standardized measures

Source: vignettes/standardization.Rmd
standardization.Rmd

A standardized measure summarises the fitted model as one evaluation of each provider: how its outcomes compare with those expected under a national norm. standardize() computes the measures of every model class in the same form; test_measure() tests a measure against a reference value on its own scale.

Indirect and direct standardization

Let \(O_i\) be provider \(i\)’s observed total (its outcomes summed, or its number of events) and \(E_i(a)\) the total its own patients would have had at a provider with effect \(a\), given the fitted risk-factor coefficients: a sum of fitted means for a logistic or linear model, the fitted intensity accumulated over the periods at risk for a Cox model. The norm \(\hat\mu\) is the median of the provider effects by default (robust to the outlying providers that are the object of the exercise), or their size-weighted mean, or a number.

Indirect standardization compares the provider’s observed total with the total its own patients would have had at the norm:

\[\mathrm{ISR}_i = \frac{O_i}{E_i(\hat\mu)}, \qquad \mathrm{ISD}_i = \frac{O_i - E_i(\hat\mu)}{m_i} .\]

The question is “did this provider’s patients do better or worse than they would have at a typical provider?”. The quantity tested is the provider effect itself.

Direct standardization applies the provider’s fitted effect to the patients of every provider, and compares the result with the norm applied to the same patients:

\[\mathrm{DSR}_i = \frac{\sum_{i'} E_{i'}(\hat\gamma_i)}{\sum_{i'} E_{i'}(\hat\mu)}, \qquad \mathrm{DSD}_i = \frac{\sum_{i'} E_{i'}(\hat\gamma_i) - \sum_{i'} E_{i'}(\hat\mu)}{n} .\]

The numerator divided by the total number of observations is the directly standardized rate of provider \(i\): the rate the whole population would have had at this provider. Two providers’ direct rates are comparable without further case-mix adjustment, which is why several measures report them. The estimand is then a population-average rate, a smooth monotone function of the provider effect, and testing it needs the transport described below.

Ratios are used for counts and times to event, differences for continuous outcomes. A ratio above 1 or a difference above 0 means more of the outcome than expected.

standardize() 

library(pprof)
d <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 60, provider_size = c(15, 60), seed = 7)
pd <- pp_data(d, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", message = FALSE)
fit <- fit_logistic_fe(pd)
ind <- standardize(fit, type = "indirect")
head(ind)
#>   provider observed expected     ratio       rate variance_expected
#> 1     P001       14 50.59789 0.2766914 0.07078564         34.629399
#> 2     P002       44 30.62439 1.4367633 0.36756549         21.551598
#> 3     P003       47 44.45907 1.0571522 0.27045002         29.016328
#> 4     P004       54 42.98972 1.2561143 0.32135027         29.179177
#> 5     P005       35 61.58077 0.5683593 0.14540270         39.925531
#> 6     P006       16 12.27364 1.3036071 0.33350031          8.507391
dir <- standardize(fit, type = "direct")
head(dir)
#>   provider observed  expected     ratio       rate variance_expected
#> 1     P001       14  597.7141 0.2993060 0.07657111          536.3201
#> 2     P002       44 3025.0487 1.5147965 0.38752866         1712.4896
#> 3     P003       47 2261.5853 1.1324914 0.28972397         1497.1159
#> 4     P004       54 2681.7483 1.3428885 0.34354961         1632.1467
#> 5     P005       35 1186.9101 0.5943466 0.15205100          959.0992
#> 6     P006       16 2766.2424 1.3851990 0.35437387         1654.4001

The columns: observed, expected, ratio, rate (the ratio times the population rate, on the 0-1 scale) and variance_expected (indirect: \(\sum N p_0(1 - p_0)\), the variance of the expected count under the null; direct: the delta-method numerator). Attributes record the type, the null value, the population size and rate.

  • null: "median" (default), "mean" (weighted by rows) or a number.
  • n_pop: the denominator of the rates; by default the number of trials among the fitted rows.
  • providers: a subset to report; the norm and the expectations always use every fitted row.

Confidence limits of the measures

Limits of the ratio and the rate are mapped from limits of the provider effect, obtained by inverting one of the tests (ci = "exact", "score", "wald" or "robust_wald"):

head(standardize(fit, type = "indirect", level = 0.95, ci = "score"))
#>   provider observed expected     ratio       rate variance_expected lower_ratio
#> 1     P001       14 50.59789 0.2766914 0.07078564         34.629399   0.1673478
#> 2     P002       44 30.62439 1.4367633 0.36756549         21.551598   1.1289012
#> 3     P003       47 44.45907 1.0571522 0.27045002         29.016328   0.8321438
#> 4     P004       54 42.98972 1.2561143 0.32135027         29.179177   1.0091884
#> 5     P005       35 61.58077 0.5683593 0.14540270         39.925531   0.4204167
#> 6     P006       16 12.27364 1.3036071 0.33350031          8.507391   0.8598169
#>   upper_ratio lower_rate upper_rate
#> 1   0.4463502 0.04281239  0.1141893
#> 2   1.7717141 0.28880551  0.4532556
#> 3   1.3092334 0.21288640  0.3349397
#> 4   1.5259656 0.25817952  0.3903860
#> 5   0.7526987 0.10755471  0.1925620
#> 6   1.8270113 0.21996598  0.4674022

The standard error of a direct rate

A direct rate is a function of one provider effect, so any standard error of \(\hat\gamma_i\) transports to it by the delta method: se_rate = numer_se / n_pop * se(gamma_i), with \(\hat\beta\) held fixed. Give the standard errors of a Wald test as gamma_se:

tst <- test(fit, statistic = "wald", variance = "robust")
dir <- standardize(fit, type = "direct", gamma_se = stats::setNames(tst$se, tst$provider))
head(dir[, c("provider", "rate", "se_rate")])
#>   provider       rate    se_rate
#> 1     P001 0.07657111 0.02144172
#> 2     P002 0.38752866 0.05324641
#> 3     P003 0.28972397 0.04118237
#> 4     P004 0.34354961 0.03785637
#> 5     P005 0.15205100 0.02336948
#> 6     P006 0.35437387 0.08554653

Testing a direct measure: test_measure()

The measures that report direct rates test the rate against the national rate on the rate scale (or on the logit scale), with the transported standard error. test_measure() is the measure-level z test \(z_i = [g(M_i) - g(M_{ref})] / [g'(M_i)\, SE_i]\) with \(g\) the identity, the logit or the log:

mt <- test_measure(estimate = dir$rate, se = dir$se_rate,
                   reference = attr(dir, "population_rate"), transform = "logit",
                   providers = dir$provider)
head(mt)
#>   provider   estimate         se reference estimate_t      se_t reference_t
#> 1     P001 0.07657111 0.02144172 0.2558288 -2.4898739 0.3032432   -1.067762
#> 2     P002 0.38752866 0.05324641 0.2558288 -0.4577124 0.2243369   -1.067762
#> 3     P003 0.28972397 0.04118237 0.2558288 -0.8967250 0.2001243   -1.067762
#> 4     P004 0.34354961 0.03785637 0.2558288 -0.6475156 0.1678601   -1.067762
#> 5     P005 0.15205100 0.02336948 0.2558288 -1.7186045 0.1812550   -1.067762
#> 6     P006 0.35437387 0.08554653 0.2558288 -0.5998681 0.3739036   -1.067762
#>            z            p flag      lower     upper    lower_t     upper_t
#> 1 -4.6896726 2.736426e-06   -1 0.04376289 0.1306154 -3.0842198 -1.89552808
#> 2  2.7193474 6.541087e-03    1 0.28958414 0.4954951 -0.8974046 -0.01802007
#> 3  0.8546557 3.927418e-01    0 0.21602866 0.3764864 -1.2889614 -0.50448868
#> 4  2.5035532 1.229532e-02    1 0.27358375 0.4210375 -0.9765154 -0.31851575
#> 5 -3.5907544 3.297222e-04   -1 0.11166379 0.2036962 -2.0738578 -1.36335129
#> 6  1.2513769 2.107970e-01    0 0.20871218 0.5331935 -1.3327056  0.13296939
table(mt$flag)
#> 
#> -1  0  1 
#> 17 28 15

Its null distribution is \(N(\text{location}, \text{scale}^2)\): the theoretical null by default, a known inflation such as scale = 1.8, or an empirical null through null_model (see Reference distributions). The intervals invert the test and are mapped back to the measure scale.

Continuous outcomes

For a linear fit the measures are differences: indirect \((O_i - E_i)/m_i\), direct relative to the population mean of the effects.

dc <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 40, type = "continuous", seed = 8)
pc <- pp_data(dc, y = "y", x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider",
              patient = "patient", message = FALSE)
head(standardize(fit_linear_fe(pc)))
#>   provider    observed  expected difference
#> 1     P001  -57.119267 -28.33962 -0.1998587
#> 2     P002    7.166393 -13.64698  0.1118998
#> 3     P003   11.282420 -23.39783  0.3181675
#> 4     P004   56.397734 -24.26554  0.9379450
#> 5     P005 -109.383890 -11.77728 -0.5483518
#> 6     P006   85.828761 -16.77811  0.5965516

Survival outcomes

For a Cox fit the indirect measure is the observed-to-expected ratio \(O_j / E_j\) with \(E_j\) the events expected at the national baseline for the provider’s own records, together with the person-time (the grouping variable of the survival measures’ empirical null); the direct measure is \(E^{(j)} / O\) with \(E^{(j)}\) the events expected if every patient had provider \(j\)’s own baseline, computed from the risk-set sums.

s <- sim_kecc(n_providers = 60, provider_size = c(15, 60), type = "survival", seed = 9)
ps <- pp_data(s, x = c("x1", "x2", "x3"), provider = "provider", patient = "patient",
              time = "stop", start = "start", event = "event", cutoff = 0, message = FALSE)
cox <- fit_cox(ps)
head(standardize(cox))
#>   provider observed  expected      ratio person_time
#> 1     P001        7 11.198024 0.62511029    17.76226
#> 2     P002        8 22.315135 0.35850108    41.75757
#> 3     P003        9 14.113514 0.63768669    29.99035
#> 4     P004       11  6.652873 1.65342101    10.98683
#> 5     P005       10 13.595800 0.73552128    24.77177
#> 6     P006        2 31.797469 0.06289809    54.36686
head(standardize(cox, type = "direct"))
#>   provider observed   expected      ratio n_pop
#> 1     P001     1102  666.21886 0.60455432  8081
#> 2     P002     1102  402.91185 0.36561873  8081
#> 3     P003     1102  776.90991 0.70499992  8081
#> 4     P004     1102 1648.87585 1.49625758  8081
#> 5     P005     1102  731.20286 0.66352346  8081
#> 6     P006     1102   62.61549 0.05681986  8081

The ratios of a Cox fit are tested by test(cox), which treats the observed count as Poisson with the expected count as its mean (see Tests of provider effects).

An arbitrary standard population

direct_expectation() evaluates the direct numerator for any provider effects and any standard population (a linear predictor and trials per row), for instance a national population from another year:

direct_expectation(gamma = coef(fit)$gamma[1:3], linear_predictor = fit$linear_predictor)
#>    expected  variance
#> 1  597.7141  536.3201
#> 2 3025.0487 1712.4896
#> 3 2261.5853 1497.1159

Reference

He K (2019). Indirect and direct standardization for evaluating transplant centers. Journal of Hospital Administration, 8(1), 9-14.
